mixed-drop.title: A Mixed Drop
mixed-drop.hook: Man was created from a “mixed drop”: two cells from two parents fuse into one.
mixed-drop.science.0: A human life begins when a sperm and an egg fuse into a single cell, the zygote, which holds 23 chromosomes from each parent. Karl Ernst von Baer found the mammalian egg in 1827, Oscar Hertwig watched fertilisation in 1875, and in 1956 Joe Hin Tjio and Albert Levan established that humans have 46 chromosomes.
mixed-drop.science.1: The organs that make sperm and eggs begin to form high in the abdomen, beside the kidneys and near the backbone, before they descend. They keep their blood supply and nerves from up there, which is why the testes' artery arises from the aorta close to the kidneys.
mixed-drop.stats.0.label: Human chromosomes, 23 from each parent (1956)
mixed-drop.stats.1.label: Fertilisation first watched (Hertwig)
mixed-drop.proof.0.title: Von Baer: the mammalian egg
mixed-drop.proof.0.text: Karl Ernst von Baer discovers the egg cell of mammals in a dog's ovary.
mixed-drop.proof.1.title: Hertwig: fertilisation seen
mixed-drop.proof.1.text: Oscar Hertwig watches a sperm enter a sea-urchin egg and the two nuclei fuse.
mixed-drop.proof.1.cap: Fertilisation: sperm and egg fuse into a zygote.
mixed-drop.proof.2.title: Tjio and Levan: 46 chromosomes
mixed-drop.proof.2.text: Joe Hin Tjio and Albert Levan establish that humans have 46 chromosomes, 23 from each parent.
mixed-drop.fit.0: “Mixed” (amshāj) matches two sets of genes, one from each parent, joined in the first cell.
mixed-drop.fit.1: The organs that make sperm and eggs begin beside the kidneys, near the backbone and ribs, before they descend.
mixed-drop.gap.0: Classical commentators read amshāj as the mixing of male and female fluids, or of the body's humours; the gametes reading is modern.
mixed-drop.gap.1: Ṣulb and tarāʾib may mean the loins and chest generally, so “between” is read loosely.
mixed-drop.gap.2: Dāfiq (gushing) describes the emission; it is not a statement about embryology.
mixed-drop.media.0.cap: Fertilisation: sperm and egg fuse into a zygote.
mixed-drop.media.1.cap: A human egg cell surrounded by other cells.
breastfeeding-two-years.title: Two Years of Nursing, Six Months of Pregnancy
breastfeeding-two-years.hook: Two full years of nursing, and a pregnancy of at least six months: numbers that health bodies and neonatologists use today.
breastfeeding-two-years.science.0: The World Health Organization and UNICEF recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months and continued breastfeeding, alongside other foods, up to two years or beyond. A 2016 Lancet series estimated that universal breastfeeding could prevent about 823,000 child deaths a year.
breastfeeding-two-years.science.1: Verse 46:15 gives pregnancy and weaning together as thirty months. Subtract the two years of nursing (24 months) and six months are left: the reasoning of Ali ibn Abi Talib, approved by Uthman and the Companions, for the minimum length of a pregnancy.
breastfeeding-two-years.science.2: Modern intensive care has moved the limit of survival to about that point. In recent US hospital figures, about 25% of babies born at 22 weeks, 53% at 23 weeks and 71% at 24 weeks survive.
breastfeeding-two-years.stats.0.label: WHO: continue breastfeeding to at least two years
breastfeeding-two-years.stats.1.label: Exclusive breastfeeding recommended
breastfeeding-two-years.stats.2.label: Survival of babies born at 24 weeks in modern intensive care
breastfeeding-two-years.proof.0.title: Ali's deduction
breastfeeding-two-years.proof.0.text: When a woman gives birth six months after marriage and the case comes to Uthman, Ali ibn Abi Talib reasons from 46:15 (thirty months) and 2:233 (two years of nursing) that a pregnancy can last six months. Uthman and the Companions accept it.
breastfeeding-two-years.proof.1.title: Tarnier's incubator
breastfeeding-two-years.proof.1.text: Étienne Tarnier introduces the incubator for premature babies at a Paris maternity hospital. Pierre Budin builds on it, and survival of tiny babies begins to rise.
breastfeeding-two-years.proof.1.cap: An 1890 incubator for premature babies (Wellcome Collection).
breastfeeding-two-years.proof.2.title: Surfactant
breastfeeding-two-years.proof.2.text: Tetsurō Fujiwara treats premature babies with surfactant, the substance that keeps the lungs open. Survival at 24 weeks and earlier climbs.
breastfeeding-two-years.proof.3.title: WHO and UNICEF guidance
breastfeeding-two-years.proof.3.text: The WHO and UNICEF's Global Strategy recommends exclusive breastfeeding for six months and continued breastfeeding to two years or beyond.
breastfeeding-two-years.proof.3.cap: A painting of a mother nursing her child.
breastfeeding-two-years.proof.4.title: The Lancet's estimate
breastfeeding-two-years.proof.4.text: A Lancet series led by Cesar Victora estimates that universal breastfeeding could prevent about 823,000 child deaths a year.
breastfeeding-two-years.fit.0: Two complete years (ḥawlayn kāmilayn) of nursing matches the WHO advice to continue breastfeeding to at least two years.
breastfeeding-two-years.fit.1: A minimum pregnancy of six months (30 minus 24) is close to today's limit of survival, around 22 to 24 weeks.
breastfeeding-two-years.gap.0: 2:233 gives two years as the full term for those who wish it and allows it to be shortened by agreement: it is not a medical guideline.
breastfeeding-two-years.gap.1: Survival at that stage needs intensive care, and many survivors face long-term difficulties.
breastfeeding-two-years.gap.2: Six months is about 26 weeks; survival is possible earlier only in modern hospitals.
breastfeeding-two-years.media.0.cap: A painting of a mother nursing her child.
breastfeeding-two-years.media.1.cap: An 1890 incubator for premature babies (Wellcome Collection).
skin-pain.title: Skins Replaced to Feel the Pain
skin-pain.hook: “Every time their skins are burned, We replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment”: pain is felt in the skin.
skin-pain.science.0: Pain is sensed by nociceptors, free nerve endings that fill the skin. In 1906 Charles Sherrington gave them their name, in 1969 Bessou and Perl recorded from single nociceptor fibres, and in 1997 David Julius's lab found the receptor that senses painful heat and the burn of chilli peppers (TRPV1). Julius and Ardem Patapoutian won the 2021 Nobel Prize for finding the receptors for heat, cold and touch.
skin-pain.science.1: A very deep burn can destroy the nerve endings, so the burned spot itself may feel little, while the edges hurt terribly. Pain depends on living nerve endings in the skin, which is the point people draw from this verse.
skin-pain.stats.0.label: “Nociceptor” named (Sherrington)
skin-pain.stats.1.label: Heat and pain receptor TRPV1 found (Julius)
skin-pain.stats.2.label: Nobel Prize for temperature and touch receptors
skin-pain.proof.0.title: Sherrington names the nociceptor
skin-pain.proof.0.text: Charles Sherrington coins “nociceptor” for a nerve ending that responds to damaging stimuli.
skin-pain.proof.1.title: Bessou and Perl: one fibre at a time
skin-pain.proof.1.text: Pierre Bessou and Edward Perl record from single nerve fibres in the skin that respond only to damaging heat and pressure.
skin-pain.proof.2.title: Julius: the receptor for painful heat
skin-pain.proof.2.text: David Julius's lab finds TRPV1, the receptor that senses painful heat and the burn of chilli peppers (capsaicin).
skin-pain.proof.2.cap: Chilli peppers: capsaicin activates the same receptor that senses painful heat.
skin-pain.proof.3.title: Nobel Prize
skin-pain.proof.3.text: David Julius and Ardem Patapoutian receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering the receptors for temperature and touch.
skin-pain.fit.0: The verse ties pain to the skin, and the skin is packed with pain receptors.
skin-pain.fit.1: Pain depends on living nerve endings, and deep burns destroy them, so fresh skin means renewed pain.
skin-pain.gap.0: The verse describes punishment in the hereafter, not physiology.
skin-pain.gap.1: Classical commentators read “replacing the skins” as making the punishment endless.
skin-pain.gap.2: Pain is not only in the skin: muscles, joints and organs feel pain too.
skin-pain.media.0.cap: Chilli peppers: capsaicin activates the same receptor that senses painful heat.
skin-pain.media.1.cap: Sensory nerve endings among the cells of the skin.
forelock-brain.title: The Lying, Sinful Forelock
forelock-brain.hook: “We will seize him by the forelock, a lying, sinful forelock”: the front of the head, where deceit is planned.
forelock-brain.science.0: The part of the brain behind the forehead, the prefrontal cortex, plans, weighs choices and holds back impulses. In 1848 an iron rod passed through the front of Phineas Gage's brain; he survived, but his judgment and self-control changed so much that friends said he was no longer himself.
forelock-brain.science.1: Brain-scan studies since 2001 (Spence, Langleben and others) find that lying keeps the prefrontal cortex especially busy, because a lie means holding the truth in mind while building something false. Damage there, studied by Antonio Damasio and others, can wreck moral and social judgment.
forelock-brain.stats.0.label: Phineas Gage's frontal-lobe injury
forelock-brain.stats.1.label: First brain-scan studies of lying
forelock-brain.proof.0.title: Phineas Gage
forelock-brain.proof.0.text: An iron rod passes through the front of Phineas Gage's brain. He survives, but his judgment and self-control change so much that friends say he is no longer himself. His doctor, John Harlow, writes up the case.
forelock-brain.proof.0.cap: Phineas Gage holding the iron rod that injured him.
forelock-brain.proof.1.title: Damasio: when the front is damaged
forelock-brain.proof.1.text: Antonio Damasio's Descartes' Error draws together cases of damage to the front of the brain that leave intelligence intact but wreck social and moral judgment.
forelock-brain.proof.2.title: Scans of lying
forelock-brain.proof.2.text: Sean Spence and Daniel Langleben and their teams use brain scans to show that lying keeps the prefrontal cortex especially busy.
forelock-brain.proof.2.cap: The prefrontal cortex at the front of the brain.
forelock-brain.fit.0: The verse names the front of the head as the seat of lying and wrongdoing; the front of the brain is where deliberate deceit and self-control are handled.
forelock-brain.gap.0: Nāṣiyah means the forelock, the hair at the front of the head, and the verse pictures a person seized by it as a mark of humiliation.
forelock-brain.gap.1: “Lying, sinful forelock” is a figure for the person; the brain reading is modern.
forelock-brain.gap.2: Lying is not confined to one brain area, and scans are not reliable lie detectors.

forelock-brain.media.1.cap: The prefrontal cortex highlighted on the brain.
moon-phases.title: The Moon's Stages
moon-phases.hook: The Moon has stages, and the last is “like an old date-palm stalk”: the thin, curved crescent.
moon-phases.science.0: The Moon shines only by sunlight, and we see different amounts of its lit half as it circles the Earth. One full cycle of phases takes 29.53 days. In its last days the waning crescent is a thin, curved sliver, very like the dried, hooked stalk that a date cluster leaves on the palm.
moon-phases.science.1: The cycle has been used to count time for thousands of years. Twelve lunar months make a year of about 354 days, so the lunar calendar drifts through the seasons: 33 lunar years are almost exactly 32 solar years.
moon-phases.science.2: Galileo drew the Moon through a telescope in 1609–10, and Newton explained its orbit in 1687. In 1969 Apollo 11 left a reflector on the surface, and laser pulses have measured the Moon's distance to within centimetres ever since.
moon-phases.stats.0.label: One cycle of the Moon's phases
moon-phases.stats.1.label: A lunar year of twelve months
moon-phases.stats.2.label: Lunar years that equal solar years
moon-phases.proof.0.title: Meton: 19 years, 235 months
moon-phases.proof.0.text: The Athenian astronomer Meton notes that 19 solar years equal almost exactly 235 lunar months, a way to keep the Moon's calendar in step with the seasons.
moon-phases.proof.1.title: The Hijri calendar
moon-phases.proof.1.text: Caliph Umar introduces a calendar of purely lunar months, counted from the Hijra. Each month begins with the sighting of the new crescent.
moon-phases.proof.2.title: Galileo watches the Moon
moon-phases.proof.2.text: Galileo points a telescope at the Moon and draws its mountains, craters and phases.
moon-phases.proof.2.cap: Galileo's drawings of the Moon in its phases.
moon-phases.proof.3.title: A mirror on the Moon
moon-phases.proof.3.text: Apollo 11 leaves a laser reflector on the surface; laser pulses have measured the Moon's distance to within centimetres ever since.
moon-phases.fit.0: “Manāzil” (stations) matches the Moon's daily positions through the cycle, and the last thin curved crescent is well described by an old date-palm stalk.
moon-phases.fit.1: 2:189 says the crescents are for measuring time, and lunar months do time the Islamic calendar.
moon-phases.gap.0: This is naked-eye observation; Babylonians and Greeks described the same phases.
moon-phases.gap.1: The verse does not say why the Moon has phases.
moon-phases.gap.2: The date-palm image is a picture from Arabian life, not a measurement.
moon-phases.media.1.cap: Galileo's drawings of the Moon in its phases.
moon-phases.media.2.cap: NASA: a full year of the Moon's phases.
night-strip-day.title: Night Is the Default
night-strip-day.hook: “We strip the day from the night”: darkness is what space is like, and daylight is only a thin layer around the Earth.
night-strip-day.science.0: Away from the Earth, the sky is black even with the Sun shining: an astronaut sees a blazing Sun in a black sky. The bright blue daytime sky exists only because air scatters sunlight, an effect Lord Rayleigh explained in 1871.
night-strip-day.science.1: That layer of air is thin. The conventional edge of space, the Kármán line, is about 100 km up, on a planet 12,742 km across. In 1961 Yuri Gagarin reported that the sky above the air was very dark.
night-strip-day.science.2: So the picture of day as a thin layer stripped off a background of darkness is a fair description of what astronauts see.
night-strip-day.stats.0.label: Rayleigh explains the blue sky
night-strip-day.stats.1.label: Height of the layer of air that lights the sky by day
night-strip-day.stats.2.label: Gagarin sees a very dark sky above the air
night-strip-day.proof.0.title: Rayleigh: why the sky is blue
night-strip-day.proof.0.text: Lord Rayleigh works out that air scatters short (blue) wavelengths of sunlight far more than long ones, so the daytime sky is blue and the sunset red.
night-strip-day.proof.1.title: The first photograph from space
night-strip-day.proof.1.text: A captured V-2 rocket, launched from New Mexico, takes photographs of the Earth from about 105 km up, with a black sky above.
night-strip-day.proof.2.title: Gagarin
night-strip-day.proof.2.text: Yuri Gagarin, the first person in space, reports that the sky above the air is very dark and the Earth bluish.
night-strip-day.proof.3.title: Apollo 8
night-strip-day.proof.3.text: Astronauts photograph the Earth, a bright globe against a black sky.
night-strip-day.proof.3.cap: The first Earthrise photographed by humans (Apollo 8).
night-strip-day.fit.0: Day looks like a thin layer “stripped” from a background of darkness, as seen from space.
night-strip-day.fit.1: When the day is withdrawn, people are “in darkness”, as at sunset.
night-strip-day.gap.0: The verse is usually read as a sign of nightfall, not as a statement about space.
night-strip-day.gap.2: “Naslakhu” (to peel off a hide) may be a vivid picture with no scientific claim.

shooting-stars.title: Lamps and Missiles in the Sky
shooting-stars.hook: The nearest heaven is adorned with “lamps” that are also “missiles”: shooting stars, grains of dust burning up.
shooting-stars.science.0: A shooting star is not a star. It is a grain of dust or rock, mostly the size of sand or a pea, hitting the atmosphere at 11 to 72 km/s and burning up in a bright streak.
shooting-stars.science.1: Ernst Chladni argued in 1794 that such things come from space. In 1833 Denison Olmsted showed that the Leonid meteors radiate from one point in the sky, so they must come from space. In 1866 Giovanni Schiaparelli showed that the Perseid meteors travel the orbit of Comet Swift–Tuttle: meteor showers are trails of comet dust that the Earth crosses each year.
shooting-stars.stats.0.label: Speed of meteoroids entering the air
shooting-stars.stats.1.label: Perseids traced to a comet (Schiaparelli)
shooting-stars.proof.0.title: Chladni: they fall from space
shooting-stars.proof.0.text: Ernst Chladni argues that masses of stone and iron fall from space. Scientists doubt him for years, until stones fall at L'Aigle, France, in 1803.
shooting-stars.proof.1.title: Olmsted: the Leonid storm
shooting-stars.proof.1.text: After a night of thousands of meteors, Denison Olmsted shows that they radiate from a single point among the stars, so they must come from space, not from the air.
shooting-stars.proof.2.title: Schiaparelli: meteors and comets
shooting-stars.proof.2.text: Giovanni Schiaparelli shows that the Perseid meteors follow the orbit of Comet Swift–Tuttle. A meteor shower is a trail of comet dust that the Earth crosses each year.
shooting-stars.proof.2.cap: Perseid meteors streaking across the sky.
shooting-stars.fit.0: Shooting stars are bright streaks in the nearest sky, and they are hot flames of burning dust.
shooting-stars.fit.1: “Rujūm” (things cast) fits meteors hurled into the air.
shooting-stars.gap.0: The verses say the missiles are for devils that listen in; that purpose is a matter of faith, not astronomy.
shooting-stars.gap.1: Classical commentators disagreed on whether the “lamps” and the “missiles” are the same thing.
shooting-stars.media.0.cap: Perseid meteors streaking across the sky.
shooting-stars.media.1.cap: The glowing trail of a meteor.
